name: Pimpama
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

earlier_scan.note: Extinct SE-Queensland Pama-Nyungan; Glottolog cites only Jefferies 2011 and Crowley 1978 subclassification comments; wordlist-level record.

new_statements.quote: You should note that the first syllable of a word is usually stressed and clear, except when there is a long vowel elsewhere in the word, which then gets the primary stress, and the first syllable is less clear. [p. 14] ... Unstressed vowels in the language lose their 'colour', as they do in English. Long vowels (all the ones with h written after them) are stressed; otherwise the first syllable of a word is stressed. There are never (or almost never) two long vowels in a row. [p. 16]
new_statements.citation: Sharpe, Margaret C. 1998. Dictionary of Yugambeh (including neighbouring dialects). Pacific Linguistics C-139. Canberra: Australian National University. Pronunciation guide, pp. 14 and 16.
new_statements.locator: p. 14 (PDF page 34) and p. 16 (PDF page 36), 'Pronunciation guide' (pp. 13-21)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (244 pp., text; extracted text, no scanned needed). Both quoted passages are verbatim at the stated locators: printed p. 14 = p. 34, "You should note that the first syllable of a word is usually stressed and clear, except when there is a long vowel elsewhere in the word, which then gets the primary stress, and the first syllable is less clear." (followed by the u-dropping remark kuwaŋ > kwoŋ 'rain', bulagan > blahgan 'you plural'); printed p. 16 = p. 36, "Unstressed vowels in the language lose their 'colour', as they do in English. Long vowels (all the ones with h written after them) are stressed; otherwise the first syllable of a word is stressed. There are never (or almost never) t…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the long vowel if the word has one (at most one per word); otherwise on the first syllable. Long vowels are the only heavy syllables, so this is a weight-sensitive default-to-initial system (initial stress in the common case).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not stated by Sharpe. She quotes Watson (1943/44) on Yugumbir, p. 21: 'Accent is generally on the first syllable, and to a lesser degree, on the third', which suggests a weaker beat on the third syllable in that source.
new_statements.exceptions: Watson (quoted p. 21): when the first syllable ends in r the preceding vowel may be obscured and first and second syllables pronounced almost as one (kurii'man 'kangaroo', Burii'mpa). Sharpe notes a tendency for u to drop from an initial unstressed syllable (kuwaŋ > kwoŋ 'rain', bulagan > blahgan 'you pl.'). Sharpe 1997:372: older lists' acute accents on non-initial syllables are read as marking a long (stressed) vowel.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level, citation forms in a dictionary pronunciation guide; Sharpe calls the language 'stress-timed' with slurred unstressed syllables. On the identity of the variety: this is a statement about Yugambeh (Tweed-Albert, twee1234 / ISO xjb) 'as are the other dialects of this language', not about the Pimpama list as such; Sharpe folds Prior's 1887 Pimpama vocabulary into that dictionary as source 'ATtp' (Gold Coast area lists AT, GC, Ywh). Prior's list itself carries no stress information.
new_statements.identity_note: Pimpama [pimp1234] is known only from T. de M. M. Prior's 1887 vocabulary in Curr vol. III (No. 171, pp. 232-233). Glottolog places it as a language-level sister of Bandjalangic within Greater Bandjalangic and glosses it 'Albert-Tweed by Prior = Pimpama = Coomera = Gold Coast Bandjalang third group'; Sharpe 1997:370 reports Crowley 1978 treats it as one of three 'small Gold Coast areas', 'quite marginal'; Sharpe 1998 absorbs the same list as source 'ATtp' in her Dictionary of Yugambeh; Wikipedia (citing Davies 2022) calls it 'possibly spurious'. The stress statement quoted is Sharpe's for Yugambeh = Tweed-Albert [twee1234, ISO xjb] and its dialects, not a Pimpama-specific finding.

sources.citation: Sharpe, Margaret C. 1997. "Yugambeh-Bundjalung: what can be learnt from the dialect differences." In D. Tryon & M. Walsh (eds), Boundary rider: essays in honour of Geoffrey O'Grady, 363-392. Pacific Linguistics C-136. DOI 10.15144/PL-C136.363.
sources.note: p. 370: Crowley (1978) 'groups dialects into three small Gold Coast areas (Pimpama, quite marginal, Southport, and Burleigh Heads, lists labelled AT here)'; p. 368: Yugambeh-Bundjalung is a 'stress-timed' language; p. 372: in Watson's lists 'An acute accent indicates stress usually when it falls on other than the first syllable. By Crowley's, the Geytenbeeks' and my analysis, this indicates a long vowel in the syllable perceived as stressed.' No Pimpama-specific stress remark.

sources.note: Does not cover Pimpama or Yugambeh (zero hits; Nerang only mentioned in passing). Its stress statement (Part I 2.9: 'Stress is not significant in any of the languages dealt with in this survey', with a tendency to stress the second syllable of long words) concerns Wakka-Wakka, Gureng Gureng, Gunggari-area languages, not this one.

sources.citation: Prior, T. de M. M. 1887. "Between the Albert and Tweed Rivers" [No. 171, Prior's vocabulary]. In E. M. Curr (ed.), The Australian Race, vol. III, pp. 231-233. Melbourne: John Ferres, Government Printer.
sources.note: Nothing. Curr's half-page preamble (p. 231: smallpox, descent, finger amputation, 'meebin means Eaglehawk') and Prior's two-page vocabulary (pp. 232-233, ~120 items, 'fire, wood and camp are all rendered.. by the word wybara') contain no remark on pronunciation, accent or stress; no stress marks on the words.

sources.note: Classification Pama-Nyungan > Southeastern > New South Wales > Greater Bandjalangic (sister to Bandjalangic, not inside it). Glottolog's most extensive descriptions: Jefferies 2011 (22 pp., 'a wordlist or less') and Prior 1887 (3 pp., wordlist). Language note on Prior: 'Albert-Tweed by Prior = Pimpama = Coomera = Gold Coast Bandjalang third group'. No grammar or phonology exists for the languoid.
